title: Detect DHCP Spoofing Across Linux, Windows, and macOS
shortTitle: Detect DHCP Spoofing Across Linux, Windows, and macOS
summary: This strategy detects rogue Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) servers that hand clients a false gateway or Domain Name System (DNS) resolver in order to intercept traffic, which maps to the DHCP spoofing technique in adversary-in-the-middle activity. The telemetry needed is DHCP server and relay logging, switch or wireless controller records of DHCP snooping violations, client address assignment events, and DNS resolver metadata showing where clients actually send queries. Detection succeeds when a client's gateway or resolver changes to a value that is not in the approved infrastructure inventory. It fails in practice because networks with legitimate redundant DHCP servers, temporary lab networks and failover events produce the same pattern, so the rule must distinguish approved server media access control (MAC) addresses from everything else.

beginner.definition: A rogue DHCP server is an unauthorised device that answers when computers ask the network for an address. It can also tell the computer to use the attacker as its gateway or name resolver. This detection looks for address answers that come from a device the network does not trust.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker controls the gateway, all traffic can pass through their machine. That allows silent reading and changing of data. The attack needs no malware on the victim and works on wired and wireless networks alike. Finding it quickly limits how much traffic can be read.
howItWorks: Network devices and servers send their address assignment logs to a central platform.
The detection keeps a list of approved Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server addresses and names.
It flags any address offer or acknowledgement that comes from a device outside that list.
It also watches client network settings for a gateway or name resolver that changed to an unknown value.
It correlates both signals on the same network segment within a short time window.
An analyst checks the switch port or wireless access point that the rogue device is connected to.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel reception desk that hands out room keys. A stranger sets up a second desk near the lift and starts handing out keys too. Guests take the nearest desk and never notice. The room log then shows guests entering rooms that the real desk never assigned. This detection compares the keys in use with the desk that issued them.
takeaways: A rogue address server can silently become the path for all traffic.
The reliable sign is an address answer from a device outside the approved list.
Segment level context, such as switch port, is what turns an alert into a location.

objectives: Describe how Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol assigns addresses and settings to clients.
Explain how a rogue server redirects traffic by changing gateway or resolver values.
Identify the logging sources that record address assignment and snooping violations.
Build an allowlist of authorised address servers per network segment.
Trace a rogue server alert back to a physical switch port or access point.
dataSources: DHCP server operational logs recording offer and acknowledgement messages with server address and assigned client
Managed switch or wireless controller logs recording DHCP snooping violations and the port or access point involved
Windows DHCP client events recording lease acquisition and the gateway and DNS server values received
Passive network metadata from a network security monitor showing DHCP traffic sources per segment
DNS resolver or firewall logs showing client queries sent to a resolver address outside the approved inventory
logic: The pattern is more than one device answering address requests on one broadcast segment, or a client accepting settings from a server that is not in the approved inventory. Correlate the server hardware address and server address in the assignment event with the segment, the switch port and the client that accepted the lease, then compare against the inventory of authorised servers. Also watch the resulting client configuration: a gateway or resolver value that no approved server would hand out is strong evidence even when the assignment log is missing. The benign case is planned redundancy or a documented maintenance change where the second server is known and appears in the inventory; the malicious case is an unmanaged device on an access port, often offering a very short lease and its own address as the gateway.
pseudoQuery:
# title: DHCP Assignment from Unauthorized Server
# logsource:
#   product: linux
#   service: dhcpd
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action: 'lease_ack'
#   filter_authorized_servers:
#     server_ip:
#       - '10[.]20[.]0[.]10'
#       - '10[.]20[.]0[.]11'
#   condition: selection and not filter_authorized_servers
# level: high
falsePositives: A second production address server brought online during a planned failover or data centre migration
Temporary lab or training networks that are bridged onto a corporate segment by mistake
Virtualisation hosts running an internal address service for isolated test virtual machines
Wireless guest networks that use a separate address server which was never added to the inventory
tuningNotes: The rule only becomes usable once you have an accurate, segment-aware inventory of authorised address servers, so build that first and record the switch port or access point for each. Scope the strictest version to user access segments and data centre segments where address service should come from a small fixed set of hosts. Baseline how often legitimate leases are renewed and how often gateways change so you can suppress planned cutovers with a change window filter rather than by disabling the rule. If you narrow the rule to known segments you lose visibility on guest and operational technology networks, so keep a lower-severity variant there and review new segments quarterly.
